title: Germany invades Poland
subtitle: The invasion and the battle for time
author: Robert M. Dobo
location: Poland and the Free City of Danzig
summary: German operational superiority met Polish resistance at bridges, fortified positions and railway crossings. The opening campaign depended on how quickly formations could move, recover and respond as threats developed along several axes.
sourceMethod: Numbered citations lead to the sources below, with locators and backlinks. The account combines operational history, Polish military scholarship, museum research and contemporary documents. Kennedy’s 1956 U.S. Army study is used for identified command and operational reports; its cavalry-charge and early aviation-destruction claims are rejected. Tym supports the Mokra withdrawal and communications episode. Sudoł’s Zambrów passage quotes Datner, rather than providing independent corroboration; exact victim totals and the identity of individual guards are not asserted. Franz’s study supports the dated Jastarnia mutinies and recorded detention, without an unsupported execution claim. Disputed Wieluń times and casualties remain qualified. The principal narrative covers the opening attack and selected developments through the late-September fighting, with the October release of detainees identified as a later consequence.

sections.label: Mokra and the price of delay
The invasion becomes a European war

body:
Before dawn on September 1, 1939, German aircraft attacked the demolition installations at the Vistula bridges in Tczew. A train operation was supposed to deliver troops before Polish defenders could destroy the crossings. The attackers needed the bridges intact: vehicles, artillery and supplies could not follow an air raid across a river. Polish personnel frustrated the seizure, and during the morning the bridges were demolished. Germany had begun its invasion with immense advantages in aircraft, armour and numbers, yet at this crossing the first plan had failed. The Tczew air attack is usually placed at approximately 4:34 a.m., before the bombardment of Westerplatte. The struggle over the bridges exposed the contest that would shape the campaign. German commanders tried to reach crossings and road junctions before Polish formations could withdraw or concentrate; Polish commanders needed time to assemble reserves and connect scattered armies into a defence. A bridge destroyed at the right moment could delay pursuit. It could not stop an enemy advancing elsewhere. [1] [2] The [August pact](/articles/molotov-ribbentrop-pact-1939-08-23) had removed the prospect of Soviet opposition to Germany’s attack. Its secret protocol anticipated partition, but on September 1 the Red Army had not entered Poland and the defeat of the Polish armies remained to be achieved. This study follows Germany’s opening offensive and selected consequences through the Bzura counterattack, Warsaw’s siege and the final coastal resistance. The [next study](/articles/soviet-invasion-poland-1939-09-17) examines the second invasion, from the east. [3]

The order and the pretext

By the time German troops crossed the frontier, the machinery of aggression had been running for months. The army’s plan, Fall Weiss, aimed to destroy Poland’s armed forces before they could escape the converging German offensives. The disputes over Danzig and transit across the Polish Corridor provided the diplomatic setting, but the operational design reached far beyond a border adjustment. The destruction of Czechoslovakia earlier in the year had enlarged Germany’s southern approaches into Poland, giving military planners another direction from which to threaten the Polish rear. Their task was to exploit that geography quickly enough to prevent an effective defence from taking shape. [4] There had already been a false start. Hitler intended the offensive to begin on August 26, then postponed it after developments including the formal Anglo-Polish alliance signed on the 25th. A German commando detachment failed to receive the cancellation in time and attacked the railway route near the Jabłonków Pass. Polish resistance defeated the attempt to secure the tunnel and station for the coming army. The episode belongs to the transition between diplomacy and war, and it exposes the practical character of the preparations: the seizure of infrastructure was important enough to put small advance parties across the frontier before the main formations arrived. [5] On August 31, Hitler issued Directive No. 1 for the Conduct of the War. It specified the next day and 4:45 a.m. for the attack, including the operation against the Tczew bridges. Its opening language blamed an allegedly intolerable situation on Germany’s eastern frontier, but the document itself recorded a decision for force made in advance. The same directive restrained German action in the west, where Hitler wanted Britain and France to bear responsibility for widening the conflict. He was ordering a war against Poland while trying to control how other powers would enter it. [6] The regime’s public explanation inverted the responsibility disclosed by its own orders. SS personnel staged the Gleiwitz radio-station incident on August 31 as evidence of supposed Polish aggression, while press instructions presented German action as defensive and discouraged the term war. These measures sought to shape the interpretation of an offensive whose preparations were already complete. Their place in the chronology is decisive: the staged provocations served the policy of aggression, rather than furnishing an unforeseen reason to undertake it. [7]

Inside the diplomatic record

Proposals the ambassador never received

On the afternoon of September 1, Polish ambassador Józef Lipski told the American chargé in Berlin that he had not even been furnished with the German proposals supposedly offered as a basis for negotiation. This was Lipski’s account, recorded by the American diplomat, and it undercuts the image of a straightforward settlement rejected after normal discussions. The army was already advancing while diplomats were still documenting how the appearance of negotiation had been maintained.

[8]

Two armies, two different problems

Germany’s advantage was considerable, although campaign totals can conceal the conditions under which particular engagements were fought. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives approximately 1.5 million German troops, around sixty divisions and more than two thousand tanks for the invading force. A Polish museum estimate places the forces Poland fielded during September at about 900,000. These are broad campaign measures, not synchronized headcounts of men in their battle positions at dawn on the first day. Polish mobilization and concentration remained incomplete. Germany could choose the places where its strongest forces would strike; Poland was still assembling parts of the army with which it had to resist them. [9] [10] German strength was organized to make successive Polish positions untenable. Armoured and motorized formations could threaten crossings and communications behind a defender; infantry following them engaged bypassed troops and secured routes. Artillery, engineers, radio communications and Luftwaffe support helped the mobile formations sustain their attacks. Much of the German army still marched on foot, however, and the speed of its leading units could separate them from supply columns. The advantage lay in bringing these different forces to bear together. It was neither a wholly motorized army nor a machine free from breakdown. [4] [11] Polish infantry, artillery and antitank weapons could defeat German attacks. Cavalry formations generally used horses for movement and fought dismounted, employing machine guns, antitank rifles and 37-mm guns. Their problem was to concentrate this firepower where it was needed and then move before the next German thrust cut the routes behind them. A brigade might hold its own battlefield while losing contact with the formation on its flank. Local resistance and the deterioration of the larger defensive system were happening at the same time. [12] The air comparison was harsher. The RAF Museum sets roughly three hundred mostly obsolete Polish aircraft against more than thirteen hundred German fighters and bombers. Polish squadrons had dispersed to field airfields before the attack, so the familiar story that the Luftwaffe destroyed them on the ground at the outset is false. Their survival allowed real resistance, but dispersal could not cancel the disparity in numbers, performance and capacity to sustain operations. Germany could commit aircraft against the fighting front, transport system and targets farther inside Poland while the smaller Polish force faced difficult choices about where to expend its strength. [13] Marshal Edward Rydz-Śmigły’s armies also faced a geographical problem for which there was no painless answer. A shorter position deeper in the country would have surrendered important industrial districts, population centres and access to the sea before a serious battle. A defence near the frontier committed troops to a broad arc threatened from the west, East Prussia and the south. The Polish plan tried to defend essential territory while preserving the possibility of withdrawal and continued resistance. Its success depended on time, communications and assistance from abroad—the very conditions the German offensive was intended to disrupt. [4]

Reading the offensive

Two German army groups directed the attack. **Army Group North**, under Fedor von Bock, brought together 3rd Army in East Prussia and 4th Army in Pomerania. Georg von Küchler’s 3rd Army faced the Polish northern approaches, including the fortified position at Mława on the route toward Warsaw. Günther von Kluge’s 4th Army attacked across the Corridor, seeking to cut off Polish formations and establish land communications with East Prussia. Within 4th Army, Heinz Guderian’s XIX Corps supplied a powerful mobile striking force. The northern operation thus combined a drive into Poland with the practical need to connect two German concentration areas separated by Polish territory. [4] **Army Group South**, under Gerd von Rundstedt, contained the heavier concentration. Johannes Blaskowitz’s 8th Army advanced toward Łódź and covered the northern flank of Walther von Reichenau’s 10th Army, whose armoured concentration drove from Silesia toward the interior and Warsaw. Wilhelm List’s 14th Army operated through the southern approaches toward Kraków and farther east. These assignments formed a connected operational design: the flanking armies protected the principal advance while threatening Polish forces that might otherwise turn against it. The movement toward Warsaw therefore depended on operations extending well beyond the route of the leading armour. [4] The Polish commands were arranged around the territory they had to defend. Army Pomorze under Władysław Bortnowski covered the Corridor; Army Modlin under Emil Krukowicz-Przedrzymirski faced the threat from East Prussia. Farther west and south stood Tadeusz Kutrzeba’s Army Poznań, Juliusz Rómmel’s Army Łódź and Antoni Szylling’s Army Kraków. Army Karpaty covered the southeastern approaches, the Narew Operational Group the northeast, and Army Prusy formed the principal strategic reserve. [33] Their names are useful geographical guides, but the spaces between these forces were as consequential as their individual positions. Germany’s converging advances threatened to separate them, close their withdrawal routes and commit the reserves before those reserves were fully assembled. [4]

Slovakia made the southern threat more extensive. Its German-dependent government permitted the use of Slovak territory and committed forces of its own. Two Slovak divisions took part from September 1, attacking toward places including Bukowina Tatrzańska, Krynica and Muszyna. Their contribution was much smaller than Germany’s, but it widened the area Polish commanders had to watch and defend. The political destruction of Czechoslovakia had become an immediate military disadvantage for Poland: the southern frontier now offered an attacker opportunities that had not existed in the same form a year earlier. [14]

Crossings and strongpoints

At Tczew, the defenders’ success depended on railway workers as well as soldiers. Personnel at Szymankowo helped give warning of the German operation; the attempt to rush troops to the bridges failed, and the demolition arrangements survived sufficiently to bring the crossings down. The warning mattered because surprise would otherwise have allowed the attacker to turn a Polish railway into an invasion route before its defenders could act. German engineers and commanders now had to find other ways across the Vistula. The battle for movement began with the work of people whose ordinary responsibility was to keep trains running. [1] [2] Farther north, the battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on Westerplatte shortly before five in the morning. The Polish Military Transit Depot lay within the Free City of Danzig, and its defenders faced a concentration of firepower that appeared disproportionate to the small garrison. Major Henryk Sucharski commanded a force of a little over two hundred. The initial German assaults nevertheless failed, and the position remained in Polish hands at the end of the day. It would continue resisting until September 7. Prepared defences and disciplined fire gave a small force an ability to survive that could not be inferred simply by counting men or comparing the size of their weapons. [15] [11] Mława presented a larger obstacle. Here the principal fortified position was defended by the Polish 20th Infantry Division within Army Modlin. Küchler’s 3rd Army encountered concrete defensive works, artillery and anti-tank fire after making progress earlier in the day. German infantry attacks met strong resistance; armour brought forward to break the position also failed to secure the expected result. The fighting continued on September 2, while German forces sought opportunities to the east. The eventual threat to the defenders developed through outflanking and the deterioration of the wider position, rather than a simple repetition of the first frontal assault until Polish resistance disappeared. [16]

Mokra and the price of delay

At Mokra, northwest of Częstochowa, Colonel Julian Filipowicz’s Wołyńska Cavalry Brigade occupied ground between Army Łódź and Army Kraków. Its mission was to delay the enemy and maintain contact with neighbouring formations while the larger Polish deployment took shape. This was a professional assignment to a mobile covering force, and the terrain offered ways to carry it out. Woods restricted movement, the villages channeled approaches, and a railway embankment running along the eastern side of the position formed an obstacle to tanks. The brigade’s ability to use those features helped turn an apparent mismatch into a day of repeated German frustration. [17] The opposing 4th Panzer Division was a much stronger formation, with tanks, motorized infantry, artillery, engineers and supporting troops. Military historian Juliusz S. Tym gives its strength as 357 tanks; that is a divisional figure, not a claim that all those vehicles attacked the same Polish position simultaneously. The German advantage was therefore both substantial and more complicated than the image of a solid mass of tanks advancing against horsemen. Effective armour needed accompanying infantry and supporting fire. At several points the Polish defence exploited the vulnerability of tanks that had moved beyond adequate support, while German efforts became more coordinated as the day continued. [17] The Polish cavalry fought largely dismounted. Its anti-tank guns and artillery could engage the relatively lightly protected German vehicles, while the armoured train Śmiały added mobile firepower along the railway. Success required more than possessing the weapons: crews had to remain in action under bombardment, ammunition had to reach the guns, and threatened parts of the position needed support before they were overwhelmed. The terrain narrowed the choices available to attackers, allowing defenders to concentrate fire on approaches and openings. German assaults repeatedly entered dangerous ground without obtaining the decisive passage they needed. The brigade bought time through the use of weapons, terrain and local command. [12] By evening, ammunition shortages, casualties and the danger to neighbouring positions made withdrawal necessary. Filipowicz’s brigade disengaged in organized fashion, although some elements moved independently after dark. Juliusz S. Tym records a revealing exception: the withdrawal order did not reach Major Wacław Sokol’s IV Battalion of the 84th Infantry Regiment, which remained in the Kłobuck woods until around midnight and then rejoined the retreat. The episode shows how disrupted communication could separate a unit without its men deserting or refusing orders. Holding a position, passing a message and preserving a formation for the next day were all parts of the same defence. [17] [12]

Reading a battlefield total

A disabled tank is not always a destroyed tank

Published loss figures for Mokra vary, and a total of vehicles hit or temporarily disabled should not be presented as a count of permanent write-offs. Recovery and repair could return a tank to service. The securely established result is more useful here: the Polish brigade defeated repeated attempts at an immediate breakthrough. This account avoids turning disputed vehicle totals into an exact scoreboard.

[12] [17]
A different cavalry action helped generate the enduring propaganda story of Polish horsemen charging tanks. At Krojanty on September 1, cavalry charged German infantry and then came under fire from armoured vehicles. Retelling that encounter as a deliberate attack on tanks with sabers replaced a real engagement with a caricature of Polish backwardness. Mokra demonstrates the military reality more clearly: cavalrymen, artillery crews and an armoured train used modern weapons to check a panzer division. Their success was limited by the wider retreat, not by ignorance of what a tank could do. [10]

Measuring the advance

The opening advance varied sharply by formation and sector. Robert M. Kennedy’s U.S. Army reconstruction reports forward elements of Army Group South three to four miles inside Poland by 6 a.m., with some units reaching fifteen miles by late afternoon—approximately five to six kilometres and twenty-four kilometres respectively. These figures describe selected leading elements. They provide evidence of rapid penetration without measuring an army-wide average or the depth of securely occupied territory. Read alongside the checks at Mława and Mokra, they reveal an offensive developing through uneven progress, in which movement on one axis could alter the value of resistance on another. [11] The limits of that progress appeared in the north on **September 2**, when, according to Kennedy’s reconstruction, armoured elements of XIX Corps outran their gasoline and ammunition after crossing the Brda. Supply columns had to fight through withdrawing Polish troops to reach them. The interruption was temporary, but it reveals a consequential vulnerability within a successful advance: the route connecting the spearhead to its supplies still contained hostile forces. Operational reach consequently exceeded the security of the communications on which further movement depended. [11] By September 3, the German 3rd and 4th Armies had linked across the Corridor, severing Polish land communications with the coast and worsening Army Pomorze’s position. German forces entered Kraków on September 6. These advances brought large areas behind the leading German formations, but Polish forces remained in them, fighting or trying to escape. Each pocket required troops, ammunition and time to reduce. German commanders also had to watch the west: Britain and France were now at war with Germany, making the conclusion of the Polish campaign a strategic concern as well as an operational objective. [11] [9] Army Poznań, comparatively little engaged at the outset, retained forces with which Kutrzeba could strike the exposed northern flank of the German 8th Army. On **September 9**, his counteroffensive across the Bzura began around Łęczyca and Piątek; troops of Army Pomorze joined the fighting. Its initial success forced Germany to turn forces against a threat behind the advance toward Warsaw. The attack demonstrated that Polish commanders could identify and exploit an operational opportunity even after the frontier defence had broken down. [18] The opportunity narrowed as the surrounding situation changed. The retreat of Army Łódź undermined the prospect of a combined effort, while German redeployment threatened the Polish attackers with encirclement. Renewed fighting around Łowicz was followed by attempts to cross the Bzura and reach the Kampinos Forest. German forces concentrated against the crossing routes. Many Polish formations were destroyed or captured; others fought through to Warsaw and Modlin. Kutrzeba’s attack had forced Germany to redirect substantial forces, but it could not restore a continuous Polish front. Germany’s greater mobility now helped turn the counteroffensive into another battle for escape. [18] German armour reached Warsaw’s outskirts on **September 8**, but its early attacks failed. Fighting in a defended city restricted the freedom of movement that had carried the columns across Poland. Retreating Polish troops reinforced the capital, while civilians endured a siege that damaged homes, water supplies and other essential services. The capitulation on **September 28** therefore followed weeks of continued resistance after the first German arrival. The distinction mattered to everyone inside: reaching Warsaw had brought the war to the streets without ending the defenders’ capacity to fight or the civilians’ exposure to bombardment. [11] [9] The familiar term *Blitzkrieg*, or lightning war, can obscure this uneven campaign. German units lost contact, outran supplies and attacked without adequate support; Polish formations continued fighting after their neighbours had withdrawn. What Germany possessed was a greater ability to recover from setbacks, shift forces and impose fresh crises. Poland had fewer reserves and fewer opportunities to repair a broken connection between armies. This disparity helps explain the campaign’s speed without treating Polish defeat as inevitable at every bridge or street corner. [11] [17] The men holding the isolated Hel Peninsula faced a different crisis as the campaign neared its end. Maciej Franz’s study records that on **September 28**, soldiers of the 13th anti-landing company near Jastarnia abandoned their positions, disarmed officers and tried to reach boats with which to surrender to Germany. Military police stopped about 150 men and detained them aboard the disarmed gunboat *Komendant Piłsudski*. Franz finds no surviving evidence of a court-martial or execution; the men were released on October 1. On **September 29**, men of the 12th company at Jastarnia-Bór also left their posts and overcame a military-police detachment before a Border Protection Corps unit suppressed the mutiny. These were specific acts of collective insubordination, distinct from commanders’ decisions to withdraw or surrender exhausted formations. They qualify any picture of uniformly unbroken discipline without turning the army’s defeat into a story of general desertion. [32]

The war beyond the front

The invasion exposed civilians to violence from its first morning. Luftwaffe bombs struck Wieluń and its hospital on **September 1**. The Institute of National Remembrance’s investigation found no Polish military units in the town on the eve of the invasion or that day. Patients and hospital personnel were among those killed. The destruction sent surviving residents fleeing and made the town an early example of what German air power could inflict on people who had no military position from which to resist it. [19] The investigation did not establish a complete death toll, and historians have disputed the timing of the first raid. Its reconstruction placed that raid at 5:40 a.m.; accounts placing it an hour earlier remain prominent. Neither uncertainty changes the documented destruction of the hospital or the deaths of civilians. The exact count should remain open where the evidence is incomplete, rather than allowing an uncertain figure to displace what can be established about the attack. [19] [20] Ground troops also killed civilians in the territory they overran. At Parzymiechy and nearby Zimnowoda, south of Wieluń, Polish infantry fought on September 1 before withdrawing toward Działoszyn. Paweł Żołądek’s reconstruction from witness testimony describes German soldiers searching houses, taking inhabitants prisoner and killing civilians while fighting was still continuing in the area. Two wounded survivors of a mass shooting, Zofia Pecyna and four-year-old Zofia Biś, emerged after dark. Żołądek records that German soldiers intended to kill them too, but an officer stopped them; they received medical attention. The same record thus documents the massacre and a specific intervention that prevented further deaths. It does not establish that officer’s motives or make him representative of the forces occupying the villages. [21] German security forces pursued political and racial objectives behind the advancing armies. Einsatzgruppen—mobile units of the Security Police and Security Service—joined other SS and police formations in killing Jews and attacking people identified as potential Polish leaders. Arrests and shootings of officials, clergy and educated professionals targeted the institutions through which society might organize resistance. Jewish Poles faced additional persecution because of the regime’s antisemitism. These policies overlapped without making every victim or every perpetrator interchangeable. The [October study](/articles/german-occupation-administration-1939-10-26) follows the institutions and regulations that extended this violence into continuing occupation. [22] [23] Captivity did not reliably end a soldier’s danger. During the night of **September 13–14**, German guards opened fire on Polish prisoners held in the barracks square at Zambrów. Tomasz Sudoł reproduces Szymon Datner’s reconstruction: horses ran into the crowded enclosure, prisoners rose to avoid being trampled, and guards fired despite their being unarmed captives. The wounded were denied assistance until morning. The cause of the horses’ movement and the identity of the individual guard unit remain uncertain; Sudoł places responsibility for the detention system with the Wehrmacht. These were prisoners killed after capture, not losses in the battle that had brought them there. [24] Sudoł’s discussion also identifies a dangerous connection between the fast-moving front and German treatment of prisoners. Troops bypassed by the advance could be branded irregular fighters when they continued resisting behind German lines. That classification could then be invoked to deny them the protection accorded to captured soldiers. It explains a mechanism of criminal violence, not a lawful consequence of finding a Polish unit behind the German spearheads. [24]

The invasion becomes a European war

Britain and France had not declared war when the first day ended. Their governments demanded that Germany stop its attack and withdraw, while still testing whether diplomacy could prevent a wider conflict. The distinction mattered in Poland, where each interval of discussion was also an interval of German advance. The parliamentary record of September 1 shows the British government presenting withdrawal as the condition that could avert the consequences of its commitment to Poland. [25] Italy then proposed a conference involving the European powers. Reporting to Parliament on the evening of **September 2**, Chamberlain said that Britain could not take part while Poland remained under invasion and bombardment: German withdrawal would have to precede negotiations. The immediate question was whether Germany would relinquish the military gains over which the proposed conference was supposed to negotiate. A conference held under continuing occupation might preserve Germany’s gains while postponing the moment when its opponents acted. Consultation with France also affected the timing of the British ultimatum. [26] On **September 3**, the British demand for an assurance of withdrawal expired at eleven in the morning. Chamberlain told the Commons that Britain was at war with Germany; France entered the war later that day. These were decisions for belligerency, with consequences extending far beyond a diplomatic protest. They nevertheless did not provide the immediate offensive relief on which Polish hopes depended. The French advance in the Saar was limited, while the British Expeditionary Force began arriving in France on **September 9**. The Allies were organizing for a sustained war, with defensive preparations and economic pressure playing central roles. Poland was fighting an emergency measured in days. [27] [9] [28] The United States made a different set of decisions. Roosevelt proclaimed neutrality on **September 5**, imposing the duties of a non-belligerent state without requiring Americans to suppress their opinions or sympathies. On **September 21**, he asked Congress to repeal the arms-embargo provisions of the neutrality legislation. His proposal sought to change the rules governing trade with belligerents while keeping the United States out of the war; it was not an announcement of American military intervention, nor had the proposed repeal yet become law. American diplomacy, public sympathy and the supply question belonged to the international response, but none was equivalent to an army relieving Poland. [29] [30] Hungary’s conduct also resists a simple division between Germany’s friends and Poland’s friends. Its government pursued cooperation with Germany and had benefited from territorial revision, yet refused participation in the attack on Poland and denied the requested transit of German forces against it. It subsequently enabled Polish escape routes through Hungary toward the forces being assembled abroad. These decisions differed sharply from Slovakia’s participation in the invasion. Neighbouring governments operated under German pressure, but their responses were not identical, and those differences materially affected Polish opportunities for survival and continued resistance. [31] Germany’s campaign succeeded through the cumulative pressure of attacks along several axes, the disruption of Polish movement and the failure of effective Allied relief to arrive in time. It also exposed the limits of German coordination and the persistence of Polish resistance, from the demolished bridges at Tczew to the defence of Warsaw. While those battles continued, the [Soviet invasion on September 17](/articles/soviet-invasion-poland-1939-09-17) had closed much of the remaining eastern space. Soldiers seeking to regroup, officials trying to sustain government and refugees searching for safety now faced a second invading army.
